challenges.name: connection-pools-quiz
challenges.title: Read the lunch-peak connection outage
challenges.description: Three statements about Rice Rocket's connection outage and the PgBouncer that followed it. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Count every client of the database, not only the api: who else keeps a connection open, and which slots can an ordinary role never take?
In transaction pooling, a client keeps a server connection only for the length of one transaction. Where does a plain `SET` live, and where does the next transaction run?
Read SHOW POOLS column by column: `cl_` columns are clients of PgBouncer, `sv_` columns are its connections to PostgreSQL. Which side is short?

questions.question:
After the outage the team wants the smallest change:

```text
FATAL:  sorry, too many clients already

max_connections                = 100
superuser_reserved_connections = 3
connections from other clients  = 7    (migrate job, metrics exporter, two psql sessions)
HPA maxReplicas                = 12
node-postgres Pool({ max })    = 20
```

Statement: "Lowering the pool to `max: 8` fixes it: 12 pods x 8 = 96 connections, under max_connections 100."
questions.explanation: False. 100 is not what the api gets: 3 slots are reserved for superusers and 7 are taken by other clients, so ordinary roles have 90. 96 still fails at full scale, and the next raise of maxReplicas breaks it again. Budget = max_connections - reserved - other clients, divided by the HPA's maximum (90 / 12 = 7 per pod), or put PgBouncer in front so the pods' pools stop mapping one to one onto server connections.

questions.question:
With PgBouncer in `pool_mode = transaction`, the multi-tenant report sometimes reads the wrong schema:

```sql
-- request 1, outside any transaction
SET search_path TO tenant_42;
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;      -- tenant_42.orders
-- request 2 from the same pod, a moment later
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;      -- ERROR: relation "orders" does not exist
```

Statement: "Each transaction may run on a different server connection, so the session-level SET stayed on another connection; `SET LOCAL search_path` inside the report's transaction (or a schema-qualified name) works in transaction mode."
questions.explanation: True. In transaction mode PgBouncer hands a server connection to a client for one transaction and takes it back. A plain `SET` changes that server session, which the next transaction (maybe another client's) inherits, while this client's next query lands on a different connection. `SET LOCAL` lasts until the end of the current transaction, so it travels with the work. The same goes for session advisory locks (`pg_advisory_lock`) vs `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. The misconception is that a pod's connection stays the same server connection.

questions.question:
During the next peak the api is slow but nothing errors. PgBouncer's admin console shows (columns trimmed):

```text
pgbouncer=# SHOW POOLS;
 database | user | cl_active | cl_waiting | sv_active | sv_idle | maxwait | pool_mode
----------+------+-----------+------------+-----------+---------+---------+-------------
 rocket   | api  |        40 |         32 |        40 |       0 |       2 | transaction
```

Statement: "All 40 server connections of the pool are busy, so 32 clients wait in PgBouncer (the oldest for 2 seconds); PostgreSQL itself refused nobody."
questions.explanation: True. `sv_active 40` with `sv_idle 0` means the pool (default_pool_size 40) is fully used, and `cl_waiting 32` clients are queued inside PgBouncer; `maxwait` is how long the oldest has waited, in seconds. PostgreSQL sees only 40 connections, well under its limit. Waiting is the intended behaviour of a pool: the fix is shorter transactions or a carefully raised pool size, not more pods. The misconception is that waiting clients mean the database is rejecting connections.

challenges.name: connection-planner
challenges.title: Plan connections before you scale
challenges.description: Rice Rocket wants a check that runs before anyone raises the HPA's maxReplicas or a pool size. The editor holds `pool_planner.py` with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that `plan(case)` reports, for one scenario: the server connections the api may use (`max_connections` minus `superuser_reserved_connections` minus other clients); the connections the api opens with every pod of the HPA's maximum holding a full pool; the server connections PostgreSQL sees at peak with no PgBouncer, or with PgBouncer in session, transaction or statement mode (capped by `default_pool_size`, the rest waiting); whether PostgreSQL or PgBouncer refuses clients; and which of the api's features the pool mode breaks. The docstring at the top of the file is the exact contract.
hints: Work one scenario by hand first: 12 pods, pool 20, 6 transactions per pod at peak, PgBouncer pool 40. How many client connections, how many transactions at once, how many server connections, how many waiting?
There are three numbers to get right (available, clients, needed) and one table (which features keep state in the server session). `min()` caps the server side; the difference is the queue.

A worker fleet of 4-10 pods with `pool_max` 5 behind PgBouncer in session mode with `default_pool_size` 30: clients = 10 x 5 = 50; session mode needs one server connection per client, so needed = 50, server = min(50, 30) = 30 and 20 wait. In transaction mode with 2 transactions per pod at peak, needed = 10 x 2 = 20 and nobody waits.

tests.name: The incident: 12 pods x pool 20 straight to PostgreSQL is too many clients
Transaction mode: 72 transactions at peak, pool of 40, 32 wait; session SET and session locks break
Session mode holds a server connection per client: a pool of 100 is over the 90 available
Statement mode breaks transactions; prepared statements break without max_prepared_statements
PgBouncer refuses clients over max_client_conn; a smaller server keeps 3 slots for superusers
